'''Quarks''' are one type of [[fundamental particle]]s.

== Types ==

In the current [[standard model of particle physics]] (2022), there are 6 pairs of quarks and anti-quarks:

== Discovery ==

The existence of quarks were first hypothesised in the 1960s. The term 'quark' itself was coined by [[Person:Murray Gell-Mann|Murray Gell-Mann]], inspired by [[Person:James Joyce|James Joyce]]'s novel ''Finnegans Wake''.<ref>{{#cite:Q1942}}</ref>

A series of experiments performed at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC) and at CERN around 1970 collided high-energy electrons or neutrinos with protons. Scattering distribution from those experiments is consistent with the existence of small scattering centers in protons with charges of $\frac{2}{3}e$ or $-\frac{1}{3}e$ and spin of $\frac{1}{2}$ , consistent with the hypothesis developed a decade ago.<ref>{{#cite:Q1942}}</ref>

[[File:Proton-electron-scattering-experiment.jpeg|300px|center]]

== Quark confinement ==

To date (2022), no experiment has successfully produced an isolated quark. In current particle interaction models, this is explained by '''quark confinement''', which stipulates that quarks are always confined to a small region of space in groups of two, forming '''[[meson]]s''', or in groups of three, forming '''[[baryon]]s''' (like the familiar [[proton]] or [[neutron]]). Each quark is completely free to move around in this small space, but cannot simply "stray off" due to the presence of the strong force. A macroscopic analogy is a bola:

[[File:Bola.jpeg|300px|center]]

<blockquote>
'''[[Meson]]s''' and '''[[baryon]]s''' are together known as '''Hadrons'''.
</blockquote>
